name: Age in weeks
seoDesc: Age in weeks: work out current date from the date of birth and your age. A free everyday life calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Supply the date of birth and your age and the Age in weeks calculator solves for current date. Think of it as a shortcut for a practical question that turns up in daily life. Nothing repaints underneath you: edit a field, press Calculate, and the new answer appears. That is how you find out which input the result is sensitive to.

sections.title: How does the Age in weeks calculator work?
sections.html:
The Age in weeks calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports current date in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you give the date of birth; then you type in your age.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A calendar date. Use the picker; the answer is recalculated the moment the date changes, and the count is done date-to-date rather than by subtracting timestamps.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in weeks. The unit chip switches it to any of the 27 supported units.

sections.title: The formula behind the Age in weeks calculator
sections.html:
One relationship drives the whole page:

Current date=date of birth + your age

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• A calendar date.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Time, opening in weeks

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Age in weeks calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the date of birth and your age — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Dates are compared date to date in your own time zone, so a daylight-saving change will not shift the count by a day.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the Age in weeks calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • Dates are handled as whole calendar days in the time zone of the browser, so a birth date or a deadline is compared date to date rather than as a span of hours.
  • The unit chips cover the units listed on the page. A historical or regional unit that is missing can still be used by converting it to a listed unit first.
  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

sections.title: How do you check the answer yourself?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time — date of birth for instance — and watch which results move. A result that stays put does not depend on it.
  • Try a round value you can work out in your head. If the answer matches your mental arithmetic, the inputs are on the scale you assumed.
  • Switch the units to the ones you normally use and confirm the numbers are unchanged apart from their label; if they are not, a chip was on the wrong setting.

faq.q: What does the Age in weeks calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns current date, derived from the date of birth and your age. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Age in weeks calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the date of birth and your age, which is 2 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter your age in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Your age opens in weeks and the chip beside it offers 27 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Your age = 10 wks. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Age in weeks calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
